scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

This is a regional narrative across distinct Indigenous, Spanish colonial and United States territorial periods. Neither the 1715 nor the 1914 map boundary is treated as a founding date. The 1715 record retains a misleading legacy ID but its name and summary were corrected before this association.

Island identity was compared with the Natural Earth-derived modern Puerto Rico geometry. The associated 1715 polygon describes the main island; exact historical coastlines and inclusion of dependencies remain unverified. No successor edges are inferred.

Caguana’s 1200 to 1500 range comes from the National Historic Landmark nomination. The opening period is a selected interpretive phase, not Puerto Rico’s earliest occupation. The 1493 boundary marks European contact, not the disappearance of Taíno people.

Caguana’s excavated slabs, postholes, hearths and pottery are described separately from interpretations of ceremony and contact. The nomination’s older assumptions about chiefs’ houses, the use of stone collars and population replacement are not adopted. No archaeological object is relabelled as a known person’s possession.

The National Park Service San Juan overview supports the broad Spanish administrative sequence. Its date slips in unrelated attack accounts and Eurocentric discovery language are not adopted. Colonial coercion and resistance should not be reduced to a fort-building story; the emancipation and living-heritage items provide distinct perspectives.

The 2016 Smithsonian fieldwork account is a distinct publication from the Taíno gallery guide already used elsewhere in the atlas. This card uses the unnamed maker in the 2016 article, without importing a personal identification from another work or projecting a modern technique unchanged into every earlier century.

The school photograph was visually inspected in the browser. Its sign reads Comedor Escolar above Celia M. Diaz. The catalogue supplies Aibonito and January 1942. No menu, attendance policy, family relationships or pupils’ identities are inferred.

Maldonado’s 1993 historical abstract was read in indexed form. Only its documented programme components are used; its broad effectiveness figures are omitted. Health history is not treatment advice and does not imply equal access or that colonial medicine solved all sanitation problems.

The 2022 coffee interview describes project origins and aspirations. No harvest quantity, nutritional claim or completed documentary outcome is inferred. The family and teaching claims are specific to the reported examples.

The Smithsonian dress account was read in its indexed version; direct access returned a server error. The coffee interview, government essay and hammock article also had direct-access failures but their full relevant indexed passages were available. Source notes do not pretend unread documents were inspected.

The 1875 diplomatic dispatch reproduces the actual 1873 law after discussing a different 1872 bill. The card uses the enacted clauses, not the proposed bill, and rejects the dispatch’s complacent view of colonial labour and racist comparisons. No compensation amount from an erroneous secondary summary is repeated.

The Law Library essay gives April 2 rather than April 12 for the Foraker Act. The card uses only the uncontested year 1900 and institutional account. Citizenship and constitutional changes are historical summaries, not individual legal determinations.

The 2007 Sacred Land account is authored by Taíno advocates. It is evidence for their stated perspectives and campaign; its chronological, legal and archaeological generalisations are not adopted as independent findings. No present-day access restriction is inferred from a 2007 report.
New prose is source-checked by its author and awaits independent historical review.
